utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Good morning, Mr. Panic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, your Excellencies. Good morning, your Excellencies, good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Good morning, witness.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yesterday we discussed very briefly, and we will continue today, the transcript of your examination-in-chief, esteemed Ms. Elliott asked you if you had seen that my demand or, rather, order or whatever, was obeyed, that our children be resettled in Divic and Kozluk. Was it the case that abandoned buildings and apartments in Divic and Kozluk were placed at the disposal only of the local population or the refugees?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were given exclusively to refugees, with perhaps a few individual exceptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Also on page 94, you were asked about the evacuation from the Serbian Municipality of Zvornik if the two municipalities had undergone transformation, would Muslims have been evacuated from the Serbian Municipality of Zvornik. In fact, were they evacuated from the Serbian municipalities or from the joint municipality? You know it was planned to have two municipalities. Do you know whether it was planned for Muslims not to live in the Serbian part?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that before the outbreak of the conflict, the population was mixed, Serbian and Muslims. After the outbreak of the conflict, the Muslims were evacuated, whereas refugees from other areas came to Zvornik as had been agreed earlier by the politicians.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one more point from the transcript. Two points. On page 93, under quotation marks, there is a reference to "our heroes from Kovacevici," did you understand that reference as ironic, as a reference to those who fled Kovacevici because the word "heroes" is under quotation marks?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see that anyone was a hero at that time, especially in the early days of the conflict. Why it is worded as "our heroes", I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If you call somebody who ran away a hero, it must be irony, or not?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, those who run are rarely heroes. Now, whether it's irony or not, I couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: One more thing we will come back to later. On page 81, you were asked whether the police secured some of the prisons and detention facilities. I want to ask you were they able to prevent a regular citizen from coming in and, more importantly, were they able to stop paramilitaries from coming in?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regular citizens never went in, in the first place. And they were unable to prevent paramilitaries because they were not strong enough. The paramilitaries were always stronger. They had combat experience from earlier wars, whereas the policemen were regular people who had simply done regular police work before the outbreak of the conflict. They were unable to cope with that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we briefly look at P325 in e-court? P325. I think it's something else. Do you remember one rally in Zvornik, organised by the Democratic Party of Federalists, Dr. Djukanovic, where Zulfikar Pasic and I took part on the occasion of the historic Muslim/Serbian agreement to stop the war? Do you recall that big rally in the summer of 1991?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember it took place, but I wasn't there. I don't know what it was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that in the entire Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Serbian side was complaining about the MUP increasing the number of policemen to the detriment of the Serbs and in favour of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the case in Zvornik as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the Serbian people were anxious that it might lead to the creation of a para-army that would confront the Serbs, like it had already happened in Croatia, organised by Tudjman? There was similarity?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, people were talking about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall or were you aware that some Muslims, with extremist inclinations, went to Croatia as volunteers to wage war against Serbs on the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. People were saying that there were some volunteers who went for training in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, that's a different question. Did you know that the SDA was sending people from Zvornik, Vlasenica and the entire area of Birac, they were sending their own members, policemen, to be trained in Croatia although we had our own training centres in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally did not know, but I heard from other people, that they did go for training to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would now like to quote something, and I'll do it in English so it would be interpreted better. Something you said in your interview with the OTP on 17 October 2002, it's 65 ter 22580, page 35. You said, and I don't know if I'm quoting correctly: [In English] "There was a joint police force in Zvornik you" -- [Interpretation] You were. [In English] You said that the deputy commander for traffic police, Adnan Karovic, mobilised only Muslims to come and to secure the SUP, the police station. You were upset by that. You said that the -- it was frustrating for you that Adam Karovic only invited Muslims from Tuzla sent there to secure the police station. [Interpretation] One quotation was from page 21 and the other from page 35. Now, let me ask you, witness, is it the case that the split in the MUP along ethnic lines started very early on, as a result of misunderstandings and the leadership in the MUP always favoured their own ethnic community?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Officially, the MUP was divided in Zvornik on 6 April, but the division started much earlier, and it's true that the man called Adnan, not Adam, Karovic called only upon Muslim policemen on that day to secure the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that there were suspicions and it was not advisable to send Serbian policemen to chase Muslim criminals in Muslim areas and villages? Do you agree that this was the reason why the police force, joint as it was, could not operate properly?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Already at that time, patrols were mixed, one Serb, one Muslim, and if the criminal concerned was Muslim, Muslim policemen handled it, and if it was a Serb criminal, or offender, Serb policemen would intervene.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said, in the transcript of this interview on page 23, that you do not know, you did not see Zvornik station receive any instructions from Pale. Can we agree that all your communications were towards the ministry along the chain of command, not towards Pale?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the work of SUP Zvornik is concerned, the communications ran normally towards the Ministry of the Interior. In the early days, communications were not working, so they were diverted through the Bijeljina centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember the Lisbon Conference and the fact that we were given the right to have our own republic and our own police force on 18 March? You must have read about it in the media. I know you were not there.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that in this statement, the interview with the OTP in 2002, you stated that you had heard rumours about Green Berets, that they were coming to town and they were dangerous?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. People were saying in Zvornik that the Patriotic league and the Green Berets had been established and that even some reserve policemen have green berets in the boots of their car, and after their regular working hours, work as security men in local communes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So effectively, the MUP was divided because the reserve force was reinforced by Muslims, because Serbs were no longer able to go to Muslim communities, and vice versa because of the Patriotic League and the Green Berets, so the division of the MUP took place long before 6 April?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't pinpoint exactly when the division effectively started but I know it started earlier than 6 April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement, in this interview with the OTP, on page 35, you say, and I'm going to read it out in English, actually, you said that this significantly contributed to the acceleration of the crisis. Actually a murder of a JNA officer and the firing at a JNA column in Sapna that that significantly contributed to it. Do you remember that happening on 5 April when, as a convoy was leaving for Yugoslavia, the local Muslims in Sapna attacked it quite unnecessarily, killing an officer and wounding some soldiers?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that happening, and I think that Vasilic Marinko and Mujic Fadil went from the SUP to carry out the on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were also aware, and you spoke about that in the Zupljanin case on 12 November, that is 65 ter 22584, on page 2974, you said that you were aware that there was a Muslim Crisis Staff that was led by Sakib Halilovic. Actually, you didn't know exactly whether he was the commander, you knew the man but you didn't know whether he was the commander of the staff but you knew that the staff had been established, right, also that it was established a lot before the Serb Crisis Staff was established?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard that it had been established but I'm not sure whether it was Sakib or Asim who was the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also said in that same transcript that you were aware that the Patriotic League had been established and the Green Berets. Did you know that there were other paramilitary formations, Muslim paramilitary formations like the Mosque Doves, the Black Swans, the Cobras and so on. Have you heard of all of these?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that such units existed, but I did not come across them. Possibly I knew them but I didn't know that they were members.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that the Muslim Crisis Staff imposed a curfew in Zvornik? You spoke about that in the Zupljanin case on page 2976, that is 65 ter 22584. Actually I'm saying all of this for the Trial Chamber, the participants. I mean this number. I don't want it to confuse you. Do you remember that you confirmed or rather that you said during that testimony that the Muslim Crisis Staff imposed a curfew in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They secured particular facilities separately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do we agree that the Serb people in the urban part of Zvornik, as well as throughout the Municipality of Zvornik, were in fear for months before the war because of this paramilitary force and because of this behaviour of the Muslim leadership? Was there fear among the Serb people and were they leaving Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stories like that started even before. Also, people were saying that the situation from the previous war would repeat itself, that Serbs would not be able to live there any more. I heard stories like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That was the Muslim position, right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said in the Zupljanin case, on page 2869, same number, you said that there was a division of the municipality, or rather that there were negotiations aimed at transforming the municipality into two. You said or actually do you agree that what existed was a purely rural and purely Muslim area and that in town there was an area that was predominantly Serb and another that was predominantly Muslim? You mentioned this river and from there onwards, the Serb municipality would start, right? Zlatica, whatever the name of the river was, Zlatica, from Zlatica towards Karakaj, that was supposed to be Serb and the rest was supposed to be Muslim, right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is what was being discussed. First there was a discussion of joint patrols that would patrol the entire region, and the other option was to have a division, that Muslim -- the Muslim part of Zvornik should go to Zlatica and then from Zlatica towards Karakaj that would be the Serb part of Zvornik. As for the surrounding villages, most of them were Serb, Lok, Pilica, Rocevici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That was on page 77 so I do apologise a bit, 2877, that was the page. All right. Of course, it's not that there would be a border there. It would be an administrative division, like in Sarajevo and elsewhere, where there are several municipalities, right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the option.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said in this interview with the OTP that you had never heard of Variant A or B, and that you did not notice that something was being implemented on the basis of that paper, right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the first time I heard about some Variant A and B, in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. 1D3939, can we please have a look at that in e-court? 1D3939. I believe we have a translation too. Could the page on the left be zoomed in for the witness? Yes, yes, that's it. I'd like to draw your attention to this decision on the proclamation of the Serb Municipality of Zvornik of 15 March 1992. Do you agree that what is written there is that the Serb Municipality of Zvornik is being proclaimed and in Article 2, that it says that it will consist of areas of local communes and urban and rural areas where the Serb people constitute a majority? So what you've been saying is that, isn't it: Where the Serbs are a majority there would be a Serb municipality and where the Muslims are a majority there would be a Muslim municipality, right? Yes, you can see it in English?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what the decision says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1693, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say in your testimony in Zupljanin, that is page 2980, that in April the Muslims started guarding buildings in the town of Zvornik itself, and that they introduced check-points where they checked people, where they asked for IDs and were searching for weapons that were being smuggled already then.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the time the Muslim population had already started securing various facilities and a few days later the Serb population started securing their own facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So there was a maximum distrust, right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As soon as they started providing security on an individual basis for their own buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 1D3666, could we see that in e-court now? Is it correct that quite a lot of people, civilians, both Muslims and Serbs, started leaving before the war, especially Serbs? They started crossing the Drina River and going to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After the conflict broke out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Panic. Yes, Ms. Elliott?

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: I believe this was admitted as P3390, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It doesn't say it's been admitted, 3390, was that yesterday? Whenever?

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: It was an associated exhibit with Mr. Panic's Stanisic and Zupljanin testimony, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Panic, you are aware of this document. It's a report dated 7 January 1993 and it has to do with 1992. I remember you mentioning that. It has to do with the work of the police in Zvornik, right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we have page 3? Please focus on this, the lower part of the page, in the month of March, there is an open split between the employees. I don't have to read it all out. You can read it yourself. And in English it's probably on page 3 or 4 as well. It has to do with the functioning of the MUP. Could we please have page 3 in English? See what it says here, between 10 and 15 March, as well as on 23 and 27 March, policemen of Muslim ethnicity were mobilised, which led the Serbs in the public security station to organise a rally that was attended by the chief of the CSB Tuzla, the chief of the milicija of the CSB Tuzla and an employee of the SDB from the CSB Tuzla. This rally was supposed to be attended by a representative of the MUP as well but he did not come. It's actually the next page in English. Do you remember that rally? Do you remember all that drama about this division and this mobilisation of the reserve force, the Muslim reserve force, an explanation was demanded, who had ordered this mobilisation of employees of Muslim ethnicity and so on?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember. That is the case of Adnan Karovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ah-hah. Thank you. Then Serb employees left the rally by way of a demonstration. Can you read all the rest of it, to the end? And it says this Muslim employee in charge of communications said that on the telephone Adnan Karovic -- can we have the next page in Serbian -- Adnan Karovic, the deputy commander of the traffic police station had given the order for mobilisation by telephone, right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have -- yes, yes. It's the next page, next paragraph, Serb employees came up with an ultimatum saying that things could not be done that way adding that if a division was necessary, it should be carried out peacefully. Is that the way it was?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please look at B down here, on 4 April, in English it also starts on this page, 6. The assistant commander and the commander who were Serbs went to a meeting of the Crisis Staff in Ugljevik to discuss further activities, right? And that is when this officer or non-commissioned officer, was killed in Sapna and another soldier was wounded, right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We are not going to dwell on this any longer and the document has been admitted anyway. So this started on 4 April?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us confirm whether this is part of what is already admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Some part of the document is written in Cyrillic and the other part Roman. I'm just checking whether -- can you upload Exhibit P3390 to confirm?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This has a number, has a date and the signature of the chief. And the number of the copy. It says it's an internal document, official secret. We could see that on the first page in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I confirm it's part of the exhibit P3390. Let us continue. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then you say that on 7 April there was a meeting in Mali Zvornik and for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, I should say that Mali Zvornik is a part of Zvornik that remained in Serbia, just across the river. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mali Zvornik is in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It was an attempt to agree on how to divide the municipality, and it was attended by representatives of Serbs and of Muslims, and then you say Arkan slapped Serb representatives about, saying, "There would be no such agreement." You said that in the Zupljanin trial on page 2877.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He slapped Dragan Spasojevic, Brano Grujic and the Muslims' president. I can't remember the man's name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that sometime from 3 or 4 April until 7 or 8, Serbs ran en masse to Karakaj and across the river to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After that incident with the killing of the officer in Sapna, a lot of the Serbs crossed over to Serbia or joined their relatives in villages further away, leaving Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said there was then an attack by Arkan on Zvornik and there was fighting with Serbian forces?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe it was on 8 April that Zvornik was attacked, and there was some but not much resistance by Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that their leadership ran away immediately after the meeting with Arkan? They left their units and that's why the resistance was so poor? They withdrew to Kula?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Even earlier on, they had disagreements in their leadership, between Asim Zubar and the other leader who was president of the municipality, and they withdrew, yes. They pulled out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said you saw, after the initial clashes, some dead bodies in civilian clothing. Do you agree that civilians also took part in the fighting and if such a person were killed, somebody else would pick up their weapon and go on? Is it true that civilian clothing, itself, did not mean that a person did not take part in combat, such as Fahrudin, Nale and similar people? Were they able to fight still wearing civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's quite possible because in the early days of the conflict, many Serbs and Muslims had weapons but had no uniforms, or they would have the top of the uniform and wear it with jeans.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then you said that after 10 days, Zvornik was practically empty. You spoke about that in your interview with the OTP, page 5 of the 65 ter 22581, but also in your evidence in Zupljanin, page 2982, you said it was empty after Arkan pulled out, Zvornik was empty. Serbs and Muslims alike had fled.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we look at 65 ter 30665? You've already said that the communications had broken down and it was very difficult to get anyone on the telephone.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. And if there was something urgent, we sent a messenger to Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about Pale and Sarajevo? You couldn't even send messengers there, the roads were blocked or rather you could take a round-about via Crni Vrh but it was risky.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We informed and reported to Bijeljina centre, and we couldn't report to Pale at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, look at this, please. This is a recorded telephone conversation of 16 April 1992 between Jesiric and Cedo Kljajic. Did you know who these people were?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never heard of Jesiric. I heard of somebody called Jesuric in Bijeljina. Also never heard of Cedo Kljajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Next page, please. In both versions. In English, we need page 3. Look at the top. Jesuric says, "So, everything is normal in Bijeljina, things are returning to normal in Zvornik," and he's saying this to Cedo Kljajic, who was for your information some sort of chief at the ministry. Probably in charge of the police. Jesuric says, "15.000 Muslims ran to Serbia, which means they are not afraid of Serbs." And Cedo Kljajic says, "They escaped to Mali Zvornik, right?" Jesuric says yes. Cedo Kljajic says, "To Serbia, they escaped to Serbia so they trust the Serbian people." Is this also consistent with your knowledge that both sides were free to run to Serbia and they did?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They went to Serbia, to Mali Zvornik, and those displaced persons we had mentioned before also went to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree, then, that the Serbian leadership had nothing against the people? Nobody tried to stop them from fleeing to Serbia, from finding shelter there. It was a conflict with the extremists who had sets up these paramilitary Muslim armies?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was even a time when the SUP issued them with permits to cross over to Serbia, the Muslims, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be MFIed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Elliott?

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We will mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D1694, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now see P1478? The diary of General Mladic. Serbian page 250, English page 252. Typewritten version. Serbian 250, English 252.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting, do you remember that the issue of volunteers was governed by law, and most of these men were first volunteers and then became renegades and paramilitaries? They would report to the Territorial Defence as volunteers, but they would not go to the front line as assigned, they would return as renegades and paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At first they joined the Territorial Defence, and then the army and the police, but then they would leave and start acting independently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at line 2, volunteer units enjoyed exceptional success led by Arkan and Seselj. Arkan's unit withdrew in orderly fashion but some others that stayed went out of control. Do you see what's written there?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This has already been admitted in its entirely, right? The whole diary? We see that already at that time Arkan withdrew immediately while other volunteer units turned into something quite different.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those were mostly units led by Pivarski, Niski, Zuca, the White Eagles, some individuals who didn't belong anywhere, they looted and ran amok in villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says also here that Captain Dragan appeared and complicated the situation and says some units formally joined the brigade but in reality they do whatever they please. Is that consistent with your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, some individuals would report to the brigade but they continued acting independently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You spoke about the situation in Kozluk. Can we call up in e-court 65 ter 12163? Is it true that you knew that Fadil Banjanovic was negotiating and working to avoid conflicts as the leader of his own community in Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Fadil Banjanovic was the leader of that community and to this day he's helping the return of those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at this, please. This is the stamp of the local commune of Kozluk and we see the header local commune of Kozluk 16 April 1992 and this is a list, if you will confirm, of Kozluk residents who had handed in weapons and ammunition?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Received pistols, carbines, hunting rifles. Carbine is not unlike the M-48 rifle except it has sights and is equipped to be a hunting weapon.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A carbine is a hunting weapon, but it can be used in combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If it has optical sights and it could be used even as a sniper rifle, correct?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we leaf through this document to see all the kinds of weapons that were turned in and the total number? Can we see the bottom? The last page. There are combined rifles, all sorts of things. In total, 87 people handed in their weapons, and we see the signatures of Fadil Banjanovic, Omer Harambasic, Jusuf Durakovic and Adnan Malhosevic or whatever, and it was received by Zoran Pazen. The names on the left are the names of the members of the Muslim panel that handed in these weapons, correct?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D1695, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there is a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm afraid not. That can be sorted out later on. Let us continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So do you remember that on one occasion they gathered asking to be allowed to leave for Tuzla, they were organised and even the Orthodox priest came and the Muftija came and they managed to talk them out of it and provided an ambulance vehicle and many other things to persuade them to stay in Zvornik? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember there were rumours about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your interview with the OTP, from 2007, that's 1D04259, you said there was no fighting in Kozluk but their safety was compromised by the paramilitaries. Is that what you stated?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was no combat and that's very fortunate, thanks to Fadil Banjanovic. If they had taken up arms there would have been losses on both sides and their safety was only at risk from paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So let me just ask this: On the second occasion, because of all these dangers they left for Subotica and then on to Europe. Is it true that almost all of them returned alive and well and that this town is, again, a Muslim town predominantly?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Most of them did return. They moved into their own homes and the town, thanks to Banjanovic, who is a deputy in the BH assembly --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is thriving.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, because of that overlapping, your question was not interpreted. Could you repeat it, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you say that the town was thriving, developing, thanks to Banjanovic?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, thanks to Fadil Banjanovic and his cooperation with the Government of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the previous answer, it was not recorded that the town remained. Were the houses kept intact? Did the refugees who used those homes, did they take good care of them and then handed them over to the Muslims who returned?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The houses were preserved and the old owners moved back in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, you said the Muslims returned. Can I know when they returned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot tell you exactly, but the people returned to Kozluk relatively soon after the war, perhaps a year or two later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: After the war. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was the situation similar with Divic, that the refugees there too preserved the homes and returned them to the old owners and that almost all of them returned, and this was another one of the predominantly and large Muslim communities in the Zvornik municipality? Correct?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is true. Most of them did return, and even the mosque was renovated, the mosque which had been destroyed earlier. It was renovated and -- and transferred to a different location.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you talk in your transcript, the interview with the Prosecutor, of 2002, on page 26, that's 65 ter 22580, that's the document I'm referring to, you said there that Arkan and the paramilitaries beat up Serb policemen and forced them to put an eagle insignia on their berets; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the insignia, the person known as Topola who introduced himself as Seselj's soldier, they beat, after the Serb police withdrew from the town into Alhos, he beat a policeman, one of them, Milanovic, Milos, I believe, even cocked his gun and prevented him from further beating these people and this was -- he did this because they actually the policemen removed the eagles from their berets and put back the five-pronged star on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It would appear that we have an error with the document we called earlier and it's very important for the witness to see this list. Could we please show it on the ELMO? Through an error, it is not in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you do have a 65 ter number now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We thought we did have it when we called for it, but apparently that's not the correct number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let us proceed and see what it is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But there is an ERN number, that is a list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that this was on 21 March 1992, that we see here a list of active-duty police and there are only 29 police officers on the list, some of whom were senior-duty officers? Could we just lift this a bit? And now, as of number 16, we see that police officers are named. So we can see on the list that there is a total of 29 police officers. Could you -- 29 police officers and number 16 through 29 were working in the field. Would this show that this was really far below the normal needs, for normal functioning of the police, for maintaining law and order?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And this was together with the traffic police. So all of these men, they were all one and the same police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Meaning the traffic police only deal with traffic issues, so would that indicate that this was really far below the necessity?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, as far as the manpower is concerned, yes, it's not enough men.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please put it down a bit? At the time in question, your name appears here as the deputy commander, correct?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, for 15 or 20 days, before Momcilo Maric came from Tuzla, who then took over, and he was the deputy and I was assistant commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we now -- I would like to tender this document. There is very little to be translated. Most of this consists of names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes? Ms. Elliott?

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: We have a translation here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then it will be admitted as Exhibit D1696. Did you have the 65 ter number for that?

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, it doesn't have a 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, was this the reason why you were prompted to say, in the interview of 2002, on page 39, 65 ter 22580, that this -- did this prompt you to say that the existence of the police at the time was totally useless because the paramilitary forces were there and they did not allow any work to be done by the police, and if police officers were in -- disobedient, if they failed to act upon their orders, that they would be beaten up and that Zekic was beaten up by Gogic, himself, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The existence of the police was pointless because it was unable to do anything, correct?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as the police, the active duty police was concerned, there was a very small number of them and there was a far greater number of paramilitaries who had been at various battlefields, they were accustomed to fighting and all kinds of combat and the police was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 30 of the same interview, you say that there were occasions where paramilitaries would send the police, force them to go to the front line and they, themselves, would remain in the town and then go mistreating and harassing both Serbs and non-Serbs, that they issued orders to the police, that they sent the police to the front line, whereas they themselves remained in the rear and then went on harassing the citizens regardless of their ethnicity or faith?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was especially the case in the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that Zuca even introduced a wartime tribunal, court, and that the police had to implement his, Gogic's, orders? Is that correct? You also speak about this in your interview of 2002 on page 53.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Zuca actually established a court martial of sorts, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you agree that the municipality also introduced and declared a state of imminent threat of war and general mobilisation, and that this was in contravention of their powers and they did this because they did not -- they were -- they had lost contact with the central authorities? These were, in fact, the competencies of the republic, correct?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It did take all these steps that you mentioned, but I don't know if it had any contacts with republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But would you agree with me that the municipality did not have the authority to declare mobilisation, to declare a state of war, it did not have the competence to carry out any of these state functions unless it was completely cut off from the state?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said, on page 30 that there was a lot of tension between the paramilitaries and parapolice and then on page 33 of the same document, you go on to say that special passes were issued that allowed people, and this was done at Alhos at first and then later on on the premises of the MUP, that allowed the civilians in Zvornik, both Muslims and Serbs, to move freely through check-points and that at first nothing bad happened if a person had a pass, but that then later on the paramilitary forces just introduced their own rules; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the same page, you say that the police usually allowed these people through or advised them to stay in a certain area for their own security and that this was the case with both Serbs and Muslims; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And this was because of the threats from the paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page -- in the Stojan Zupljanin transcript on page 2896 you say that these paramilitaries captured people and established prisons. In other words they had prisons, they had an armed force, and they even had a court martial; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all the prisons, both at the beginning and later on, were established by paramilitary forces, and there were some military police prisons, but in the end, only very late, the police took over control of these prisons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you're talking about the time when the paramilitaries had already been expelled from there. This happened after they had been driven away. While they were there, no one could take over; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. None of us, or the military police, were able to get into those prisons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you say that in the second half of May, you said this in your same testimony at page 2688, that even when the brigade was established, the Zvornik Brigade, Zuca tried for a while to subjugate it, to put it under his control for a while; is that correct? That he wanted to impose himself on them and to be in control of them and command them as well by force? [In English] "At some point, Zuca took over by force and was brigade commander for a while." [Interpretation] Was this brigade established out of the existing Territorial Defence of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the beginning, when he started building an armoured train in Glinica but didn't manage to, then the brigade was established and it took over.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. These prisons that they established, you say that in Alhos, there weren't any prisons. Rather, that people were kept for a very short periods of time for investigation purposes, and you said that Serbs were kept there as well. You said that you saw a Serb there who had tried to rob a bank. You said that in your interview of 2002, on page 44. Now we are talking about Alhos. So in Alhos there wasn't a prison. It was -- it was -- it was a detention facility for shorter periods of time, during which detainees were supposed to be questioned; right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as police station work is concerned, people were brought in and questioned briefly. However, I heard that paramilitary units were bringing people in there, in the beginning. As for police work, it just had to do with short detentions and questioning, and also that particular case of attempted bank robbery.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And that was a Serb, right, so they were brought in there irrespective of faith and ethnicity, right? That's what the police did?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In this same interview, on page 45 through 47, you confirmed that you never beat or killed anyone, that you never issued such orders, and that you did not even see any beatings or killings. However, you only heard about that. This is Alhos. We are talking about Alhos all the time now. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, if it is convenient, the Chamber is minded to take a bit longer break, for 35 minutes. Very well. With respect to the Prosecution's request for leave to reply to the accused's latest response regarding the ICMP, the Chamber has considered the submissions from the parties and decided to deny the request on the basis that the reply will not be addressing anything new. We will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harvey?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, just to introduce my colleague, Mr. Matthew Odgers, who is a pro bono legal assistant who has been working with my team since June and will remain with us until December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've said, and we have agreed, that you had not seen any beatings or killings, especially as far as Alhos was concerned. Do you agree that, generally speaking, there was a shortage of eyewitnesses and that these paramilitaries did try not to do things like that in front of policemen, not to commit crimes in the presence of policemen?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not in front of policemen or in front of active-duty military personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In Standard, you said; isn't that right, you mentioned that on page 50 of your 2002 statement, and also in the Zupljanin transcript, on page 2940, and in the transcript of that interview, pages 49 and 50, you actually said that what happened in standard was that three Muslims were killed and that one escaped and that the reason for that was the allegation that they had killed a man from the police company in Zvornik near the monument and then some people from the Milic company took them to a valley and then Zuca killed these men; right? One escaped, there were four of them. One escaped and three were killed; right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All three were killed in Standard, in the basement. A member of the Milic company killed them and one escaped. They were killed at the barracks in Standard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So that means that that happened in connection with some soldier from the Milic company; right? That they killed that soldier; right? Out of revenge? They killed this soldier and then the soldier's colleagues took their revenge; right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard that a soldier from Milici was killed near the monument in Zvornik and then this Milic company when they returned to Standard, they found these four Muslims there, killed three of them, one managed to escape. Karaosmanovic was the name of the people who were killed and then one person escaped.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So this person was killed in town near the monument, not at the front line, right, that Serb from the Milic company, was killed in town, not at the front line, right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In town, by the monument. In town, there wasn't any combat at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You did not report that. No one reported that incident; right? You spoke about that in this transcript, the trial of Mr. Zupljanin, 2940, 2941. Did anyone dare report that?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of us reported that, and there wasn't a need to do that because the military police was right at the entrance into the Standard building. It was the military that had committed that killing so it was the military police that was supposed to intervene.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ah-hah. So what those Muslims did was a crime against the military because the victim was a soldier; right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that these four men were brought to the barracks by military personnel and that they happened to be there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say further on that the only real prison was in Novi Izvor. Yesterday, you explained that it wasn't at the brick factory where some paramilitary had established some kind of detention facility but rather it was at the administration building in the town of Zvornik itself, the administration building of Novi Izvor close to the misdemeanours court; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said, when you testified in Mr. Zupljanin's trial, 3023 is the page reference, people were detained because of what they had committed, and that had nothing to do with their ethnic or religious backgrounds; right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's right. But there was this group of persons there who had stayed on, people who had been detained earlier on by the military police, and the military police had secured that until the civilian police had taken over.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Panic, can we say that, as far as you know how this real prison functions and the police and the misdemeanours court and so on and so forth, can we say that Muslims were not being detained because of their faith and the Serbs did not have it easy just because of their faith?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can be put that way, especially because it was the active civilian police that was guarding the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say further on that there had been incidents wherein the paramilitaries tried to get into the Novi Izvor and the regular policemen who guarded that prison were threatened with knives and guns by these paramilitaries, and you said you never heard or seen military policemen go into the prison and beat the Muslims -- sorry, sorry, a moment. This first thing you said in your evidence in Zupljanin, that paramilitaries tried to scare regular policemen into allowing them into the prison, is that correct? And you said also the policemen guarding Novi Izvor stopped that from happening?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. Because I heard that earlier, while the prison was guarded by the military police, individual paramilitaries did go into the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you mentioned one case when somebody went in to beat a Muslim as a personal revenge because that person's brother had been killed?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You also stated in the same evidence, on page 3027, that Sredo Vukovic, a regular policeman, a colleague of yours, had to reinforce the locks and boost the security in the prison in general, to stop the paramilitaries from going into the prison and mistreating the inmates; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You also stated in your interview from 2007, 1D4259, page 12, that food was brought from a hotel into this prison called Novi Izvor, that was under the control of the regular police?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your 2007 statement, page 31, you said you knew that a certain female by the name of Stojkic from Celopek had been arrested and brought to Novi Izvor and it was not the police who arrested her but Niski, Pivarski, Topola and the others. Spomenka Stojkic was the name. Was she a Serb woman?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Spomenka Stojkic was arrested by the paramilitaries. She was a Croat married to a Serb in Celopek.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that at the farm, some detainees were kept but you don't know who brought them there as detainees. You learned about it only later, after it was finished. You said that in your 27 June 2007 statement, pages 56 and 57. And that's all you know about that farm?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the cultural hall in Drinjaca, there were also certain incidents and Pivarski spent most of his time there while Niski was in the suburbs of Zvornik, such as Scemlija, Karakaj and others, right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that Drinjaca is a Serb neighbourhood in Zvornik municipality but it was cut off from the town of Zvornik by Muslim neighbourhoods that were controlled by the Muslims at the time, so you couldn't get to Drinjaca directly from Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. For about a year, you could not pass through the tunnels to Drinjaca because all sorts of explosives were laid there, and you had to go via Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You heard from some policemen that the paramilitaries, led by Pivarski had killed some people there, you said you didn't know where they were buried and some had in all likelihood run away. You said that in your 2002 interview, page 49, is that true?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You further stated in the same statement, page 45 -- sorry, in your 2007 statement, page 45, that the police made sure to get out of Zuca's way and the way of Zuca's men, and they were unable to deal with them. They were trying to stay out of trouble. You also said the police did not venture into the suburbs which they kept. The police didn't go to Drinjaca or the other suburbs controlled by Zuca and the other paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned again in the examination-in-chief, and in your statements, the Technical School in Karakaj. In your 2002 statement, pages 6 and 8, you stated that the security and control over that school were handled entirely by Repic, not the regular police. In fact, you mentioned it again in 2002, in the transcript, 9 through 12, that the policemen who were there were not under the command of the police station and yourself, they were instead given orders by these paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The whole time, the Technical School was guarded by one of our companies, but the paramilitaries went in as they pleased and when they pleased, and the police were never able to stop them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You also said, and it's on the transcript, pages 13, 14 -- I mean the transcript from 2002 -- and page 14 as well, that you toured Muslim neighbourhoods, together with Slavko Eric, to collect weapons, and you said that Muslims trusted you and Slavko; right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then you said that not even the commander, or the chief of police, were able to do anything if Zuca's men were involved in anything or had taken control of a certain location.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's true. Zuca even threatened to take over the municipality building at one point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mean the municipal administration?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Again speaking about the cultural hall in Celopek, you said in your 2007 statement, pages 85 and 86, that reserve policemen were very scared of Repic and it's highlighted in the transcript that reserve policemen had no police training and did not have a prayer in resisting Repic. They had never even fired a bullet in their lives, let alone at someone like him.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Your answer was not reflected in the transcript but I take it you said yes, Mr. Panic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We are now talking mainly about Celopek. While your reserve policemen had no training whatsoever, nor had any experience of shooting at people, Repic and his men had plenty of combat experience, much better equipped than the police; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You also said that -- that was in the 2007 transcript, page 60 -- you said the police in Celopek had received even a written order not to allow anyone in and that they are authorised to shoot at anyone who tries to come in and disturb the prisoners, but you also said that none of them dared resist Repic, in his long coat, who was carrying a long-barrelled Skorpion gun, correct?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That was on page 62 of the 2007 statement. It's in fact 62, not 60. You also described in the same document, pages 16 and 17, that, once, while in Celopek, you encountered Cvjetko Jovic who told you that the paramilitaries, Repic, Niski, Pivarski and others, were present in Celopek and they were all-powerful. Jovic said he feared Repic more than Muslim attacks, and he also said that Repic didn't care whom he killed, Muslims or Serbs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You spoke about that beginning with pages 16 and 17 in this document. Then 10, 19, 59 and 71. And you again spoke about it in your evidence in Zupljanin, page 2903. And there are two more references in the 2007 document, pages 59 and 60, and Zupljanin trial, 3013. Yes, that's right. You also said, in the same transcript of 2007, pages 59-60, that the police had neither the material resources nor the courage to arrest Repic because he was backed by Zuca's Brigade, which had more than 100 men, as I read somewhere, and which would have protected him, if necessary?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Zuca was his brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then in the same transcript, pages 59-60, you said that only the special unit was able to arrest him, and that's indeed what happened. He was detained in Sabac, in Mitrovica, where he committed suicide, and that many people actually were relieved after his death, knowing that he would no longer be coming to Zvornik, correct? That's what you said in Zupljanin on page 3013, that everyone was relieved knowing that he would no longer come there; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. Knowing Repic and what he was like, no one really cared for meeting him again later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You also said, in the 2007 transcript on page 26-27, that you did not inquire with Vasilic whether he had reported on the activities of the paramilitary groups. You didn't know anything about that - correct? - whether he had reported that to his superiors?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There were instances where active duty police officers -- please bear with me. Later on, during the conflict, active duty police officers took over and they provided security, and this was something that the commander had ordered in order to ensure greater security and protection for the detainees. You said that in the Zupljanin trial on page 3017. Are you saying that the immediately superior command level always cared for the protection and security of the detainees?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the 2006 interview, 65 ter 22581, it could be a 2007 interview -- no, 2006. On page 14, you said that there was an attempt in Divic, an attempted rape of a woman, and that this was perpetrated by a reserve police officer, that this was prevented, and that he was expelled from the police and that there was a criminal complaint filed against him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that the people from Divic could receive medical assistance in Novi Izvor and on the premises of the misdemeanours court? You said this in the Zupljanin trial on pages 3033 and 3034. So that's correct, that they had access to medical care; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a doctor, a woman, everyone called her Bela, she came to the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You also stated that no one could have access while Captain Dragan still ran this training centre, that no one was allowed access there, nor could anyone enter the premises of Hotel Vidikovac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that during a lunch, Mladic actually had verbally yelled at Captain Dragan and that after that he left Zvornik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't know. I didn't hear of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the transcript does not reflect this correctly. The witness said, "I heard of that later on. I didn't know anything about it at the time."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that correct? Was that your answer?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As for written reports on the conduct of these paramilitary units, do you consider that people were afraid to submit written reports, and do you agree that a delegation went to Pale and also to Bijeljina to report orally on that, and that this had, as its outcome, the arrest of these people?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also describe the situation in Djulici and Bijeli Potok in late May. You said that it had been agreed that Muslims from Klisa which is a village near Zvornik, were to be transferred via Bijeli Potok and Memici to Kalesija municipality; is that correct, you mentioned this in your interview of 2002 on page 6 and you also testified in Zupljanin on page 2898 regarding the same event?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On 1 June 1992, that's when that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You also said, in the 2002 transcript, on page 7, that your men did not harass the Muslims who were supposed to cross over and to go to Kalesija; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were there just in order to help them when they were boarding the vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your police station also had a department for criminal investigation for severe crimes, murder and similar, and at the head of that department was Ratko Jovicic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: They had meetings with the chief and the commander, morning meetings, but you did not attend those meetings. However, you know that there was a distribution of work among the various police departments. For instance, when a civilian called to report that a body had been found somewhere, the police would go out there and conduct an investigation, and Pero Tanic, a police officer, was in charge of sanitisation, and you speak about this in your 2007 transcript, on pages 47 to 49, and 47 to 50, correct?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Pero Tanic organised a commission which would carry out sanitisation or clearing up of the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you -- could it be said that Mr. Jovicic or rather that for every case that was reported to the police, an investigating commission would go out and conduct an investigation, an on-site investigation, regardless of who the perpetrator or the victim was?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly whether they went out in every single case, but I know that frequently both the criminal department and the State Security Service would go out, and sometimes a pathologist would accompany them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that most of these reports reached the station to the effect that there was a body found somewhere and that very infrequently there would be an eyewitness, which would mean that either they were afraid to report or there weren't any eyewitnesses?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the beginning, most of this information or reports were received over the phone, and the people would never even mention their names. They wouldn't identify themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You then go on to say, in the 2007 transcript, on pages 54-55, that Vasilic told you that it was necessary to go to Pale or Bijeljina to tell them something about that, and that this should be done more frequently in order to prevent the robberies, the shooting, and that to do that it was necessary to go to Pale or Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So how long did this go on for, this situation, that you had to actually go there in order to be able to report because there was no other way to do it?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but I believe that went on till late June or early July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No. Late July, early August, that's what the witness said; correct? And does that actually correspond to the time when the paramilitaries were arrested? Does that coincide with those events?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Zuca's unit and the others were arrested, I believe, on the 28th, going on 29 July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So your answer to my earlier question was the situation went on like that until late July and early August, that we had to go there and report on the events orally; is that correct? That it was difficult to get to Pale or even to Bijeljina and that people did not dare submit written reports. So did you say till the end of July and early August rather than till the end of June, early July?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said, I believe, up until the end of July or early August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Prior to the arrest, there was a written report by a policeman called Dragan Andan who was not from Zvornik but rather from Bijeljina. Do you consider that that is why it was easier for him to submit written reports, whereas no one in Zvornik dared do that?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragan Andan, as far as I know, was an inspector at the Ministry of the Interior, and he would conduct inspections of public security stations, he would tour the stations and conduct inspections there, and I believe that that's when he submitted these reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also said in Zupljanin on page 2908 that after -- that Vasilic was replaced by Lokancevic -- my apologies, that's 2874, page 2874 -- that he was replaced by Lokancevic and that then the police expelled and drove out Gogic's men across the Drina. You said this on page 2908. Was that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Except that the police expelled the Gogic men on the 27, 28 July, and a day or two later, Zuca's men were arrested and that's when Marinko was replaced.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So in Bijeljina, as you learned, there had been plans for this arrest and the Zvornik police was told to be careful and not let Zuca escape, and you testified about this in Zupljanin on page 2926; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The Special Police under the command of Karisik, and together with Mico Davidovic, planned this operation, they had arm-bands as a sign or mark to recognise each other, and they went to Zuca's house and arrested him there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There were also clashes with other paramilitary units, and from that time on, they were on a downward curve or, rather, the authorities reasserted their power there, and you mentioned this on pages 52 to 56 in the transcript; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I noticed that you remember the day when Gogic's men were expelled because it was your birthday, right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The 28th of July, that's when I was born.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that the reason for their arrest was mentioned on pages 54 and 56 of the transcript of 2002. Also in 2007, in the transcript or rather on page 40, the reason was not only the fact that they mistreated Minister Ostojic but also because they treated the Muslim population badly and violently, because they were out of control; right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: After that, Vasilic and Grujic were replaced in that situation, and Lokacevic was appointed and Branislav Mihajlovic was appointed commander of the station, right? You spoke about that in your statement of 2007 on page 52, and also in the Zupljanin trial, on page 2929, and 2930. So this overall crisis was that arrest of paramilitaries something that resulted in a change in the people who were in government and also at the police station?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But Mico Lokancevic is the name, not Lokacevic. So it's spelled Lokancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All the rest is correct, right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can it be said, then, that it's not that they had made any active mistakes, quite simply they were incapable of dealing with the situation regarding these paramilitaries, and after this clearing up, the new people in power were supposed to have a free hand in ensuring law and order. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As a matter of fact, they resigned themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now have a look at 1D3944? I'm going to show you a series of documents now that were passed by the authorities from the moment when the conflict broke out on 4 April, the documents that were adopted by the civilian authorities in their effort to ensure the rule of law. 1D3944 is the document I'm looking for. This is not it. Yes. Now we have the right document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: Pardon me, this English translation is not the same as the B/C/S document, but there a correct English translation available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very kind of you, Ms. Elliott.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence is also grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could print it out, shall we put it on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In order to make things easier for the translation service, we wanted to have at least something translated so that we would not be too late. I would like to ask you to go on looking at this Serbian version, Mr. Panic. Do we agree that on 21 April 1992, the provisional government of the Serb Municipality of Zvornik passed an order on determining burying sites and funeral ceremonies for individuals killed in war in the town of Zvornik and the surrounding area? It says in the Kazambasca?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kazambasca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Graveyard near Zvornik, actually can you read all of that?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please zoom in a bit? Because --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we please zoom in and could you please read paragraph 1?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 1: "The Kazambasca* graveyard near Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we have an English translation on the ELMO. You can put your question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that what is regulated here is the following, that Muslims and Serbs should be buried in a dignified manner at their cemeteries and with appropriate religious rites except for those who are taken by their families, but if the municipality is handling this, the municipality is going to do it in a dignified manner? Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to this order, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This will be admitted as Defence Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. ELLIOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, just one observation, I have no problem with the admission of this document. However the only thing that the witness confirmed is that the document says what it says. And I'm having some difficulties in reconciling Mr. Karadzic offering documents for admission on that basis today with Mr. Robinson's objections yesterday and consistent application of the guidelines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to respond, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Our position continues to be that the witness -- a document should be admitted if the witness can confirm something about its contents. So perhaps Mr. Karadzic can ask additional questions if the Chamber is not satisfied with this.
